💭 Rabbi Elazar's Dream — confirming an interpretation of Rabbi Yoḥanan

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Ownership, Timing, and Family Partnership
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 56a–56b
overview.hebrewSource: לָקַח עֲשָׂרָה עוּבָּרִין בִּמְעֵי אִמָּן — כּוּלָּן נִכְנָסִין לַדִּיר לְהִתְעַשֵּׂר
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The Gemara grounds yesterday's exemption for purchased or gifted animals in a verbal comparison to the redemption of a firstborn son, then immediately tests the analogy's limits: if one purchases ten pregnant animals while the fetuses are still in the womb, do those fetuses — once born into the buyer's ownership — still count for animal tithe? Rabbi Yoḥanan says yes, and Rabbi Elazar even reports dreaming of him to confirm the explanation. The daf also examines when an animal given as payment to a prostitute disqualifies it from tithe, distinguishing Jewish from gentile prostitutes. It closes with a new mishna: brothers or partners who haven't divided their father's estate are obligated in animal tithe but exempt from the half-shekel premium (kalbon), and vice versa once divided — generating a four-way analysis and a dispute over what counts as a genuine division.

slides.title: 👶 Deriving the Exemption from a Firstborn Son
slides.subtitle: How 'so you shall do with your oxen and your sheep' teaches animal tithe

nodes.content: 📜 Verse: 'The firstborn of your sons you shall give to Me. So you shall do with your oxen, and your sheep...' (Exodus 22:28–29)
🔗 Just as a son cannot be a firstborn if purchased or adopted, an animal owned only by purchase or gift is excluded from tithe too
❓ But why apply this to animal TITHE rather than a sin offering or peace offering or the pilgrimage burnt offering?
✅ Because like a son's redemption, animal tithe has no fixed calendar date, doesn't atone for sin, and isn't brought as a vow or gift — matching all three features uniquely

slides.title: 🐑 Ten Fetuses Purchased Before Birth
slides.subtitle: Testing whether the exemption applies from conception or from birth

lines.speaker: Question
lines.text: If the son analogy is exact, a purchased animal should NEVER be tithed — so why does Rabbi Yoḥanan say fetuses purchased in the womb DO enter the pen once born?

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: The verse says 'SO YOU SHALL DO' — the exclusion applies only from the time of 'doing,' i.e., once the animal is old enough to be offered. A fetus wasn't yet excludable at that point.

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: But a baraita says the exemption applies even to a young animal not yet old enough to sacrifice — so why not to a fetus too?

lines.speaker: Rabbi Elazar
lines.text: That baraita isn't reliable; and even if it were, it follows Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda's minority view that treats an unripe animal like a firstborn — sanctified early, sacrificed later.

callout.label: The dream:
callout.text: Rabbi Elazar reports seeing Rabbi Yoḥanan in a dream as confirmation that his explanation ('at the time of doing') correctly represents the master's teaching.

slides.title: 🚫 Payment to a Prostitute and Animal Tithe
slides.subtitle: Jewish vs. gentile prostitute makes a real halakhic difference
rows: Animal given to a JEWISH prostitute as payment
NOT disqualified — may still be sacrificed
Abaye: only a prostitute forbidden in marriage (i.e., a gentile) triggers the Deut. 23:19 prohibition
Animal given to a GENTILE prostitute
IS disqualified as 'payment of a prostitute'
Derived by verbal analogy ('abomination') from forbidden relations, where betrothal cannot take effect
Animal given then purchased back, while still a fetus
CAN enter the pen for tithe
It was never truly 'given' as payment while an unformed fetus — same logic as the purchased-fetus ruling

slides.title: 👨‍👩‍👦 Brothers, Partners, and Two Different Obligations
slides.subtitle: The new mishna's four possible combinations

boxes.title: Obligated in Kalbon Only
items: Divided the MONEY but not the animals
Still partners in livestock, but each holds his own half-shekel

boxes.title: Obligated in Both / Neither
items: Divided animals but not money: exempt from both
Divided nothing at all: obligated in animal tithe only (still one estate)

boxes.title: Obligated in Animal Tithe Only
items: Divided BOTH money and animals, then reunited as ordinary partners
Now treated like true strangers-in-partnership, not co-heirs

callout.label: Rabbi Yirmeya's structure:
callout.text: The rule flows from a single principle: partners owe the premium but not animal tithe; individual owners owe animal tithe but not the premium — everything follows from whether they still legally share the SAME estate.

slides.title: 🐐 What Counts as a Real Division?
slides.subtitle: Rav Anan, Rav Naḥman, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi Yoḥanan disagree

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rav Anan: only division by SWAPPING types (kids for goats) counts as a real division — dividing each type proportionally leaves the estate legally unified
2️⃣ Rav Naḥman disagrees: even swapping types doesn't count as a real division — reuniting still counts as pure partnership, exempt from tithe
3️⃣ Rabbi Elazar's version: the same debate, but framed around unequal-value swaps (nine large goats for ten kids)
4️⃣ Rabbi Yoḥanan takes the most lenient position: even an unequal-value swap doesn't establish a true division

summary.principle: The exemption for purchased or gifted animals derives directly from the laws of a firstborn son, but applies only 'at the time of doing' — and among partners, whether animal tithe or the half-shekel premium applies depends entirely on whether money and animals have both been genuinely divided.

flowSteps.content: 👶 Verse comparing animal tithe to redemption of a firstborn son excludes purchased/gifted animals
🐑 Fetuses purchased in the womb still enter the pen once born — exclusion applies only 'at the time of doing'

columns.content: 🚫 Only a gentile prostitute's payment disqualifies an animal from sacrifice
👨‍👩‍👦 Partners owe the kalbon; individual owners owe animal tithe — division status decides which

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: ownership status at the moment of consecration-eligibility, not at conception, determines tithe liability

quiz.q: From which halakha does the Gemara derive that a purchased or gifted animal is exempt from animal tithe?
o: The laws of the paschal offering
The laws of redeeming a firstborn son
The laws of teruma
There is no textual source; it is a rabbinic enactment
quiz.e: The Gemara derives the exemption from the juxtaposition in Exodus 22:28–29 comparing animal tithe ('so you shall do with your oxen and sheep') to the redemption of a firstborn son, who likewise must be one's own biological child, not purchased or adopted.

quiz.q: According to Rava's explanation of Rabbi Yoḥanan, why do ten fetuses purchased while still in the womb nevertheless enter the pen to be tithed once born?
o: Because fetuses are never subject to any exemption
Because the exclusionary verse ('so you shall do') applies only 'at the time of doing' — when the animal reaches an age fit for offerings — not while it was an unformed fetus
Because Rabbi Yoḥanan disagreed with the underlying exemption entirely
Because purchased fetuses are considered gifts, not purchases
quiz.e: Rava explains that the exclusion for purchased animals applies specifically 'at the time of doing,' i.e., once the animal could be brought as an offering — a fetus in the womb was not yet at that stage when purchased, so the later-born animal remains eligible for tithe.

quiz.q: According to Abaye, why does an animal given as payment to a JEWISH prostitute NOT get disqualified from being sacrificed, while an animal given to a gentile prostitute IS disqualified?
o: Jewish prostitutes are permitted by Torah law
The disqualification derives from a verbal analogy to forbidden relations where betrothal cannot take effect — which applies to a gentile prostitute, not a Jewish one
Gentile animals are always more valuable
There is no real difference between the two cases
quiz.e: Abaye derives the disqualification from a verbal analogy to forbidden sexual relations, where betrothal never takes effect — a category matching a gentile prostitute but not a Jewish one, upon whom betrothal could take effect.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, when are brothers or partners obligated in the half-shekel premium (kalbon) but EXEMPT from animal tithe?
o: When they have not divided their father's estate at all
When they divided both the money and the animals from their father's estate, and then reestablished a partnership
Only if one brother is a priest
Never — these two obligations always go together
quiz.e: The mishna teaches that once brothers fully divide both the animals and the money and then form a new partnership, they are treated as ordinary partners (obligated in the kalbon) rather than co-heirs of a single estate (which would obligate animal tithe).

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yoḥanan (the most lenient view in the dispute), does dividing an estate by giving each brother an equal mix of both large and small goats count as establishing separate, individual ownership?
o: Yes, always
No — even that kind of division does not establish that each share was his 'from the outset'
Only if done before a court
Only for firstborn sons
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan holds the most lenient position: even dividing the herd proportionally (equal types to each brother) does not establish that each brother's share was designated for him from the start, so reuniting the estate keeps them exempt from animal tithe as partners.
